parts.title: Part I – Multiple Choice Questions
parts.instructions: Part I contains 80 questions; each carries one point. Choose the best answer and blacken the letter of your choice on the answer sheet.

parts.title: Part II – Short Answer Questions
parts.instructions: Part II contains 6 questions (20 points). Write short answers on the answer sheet.

source.prepared_by: Department of Agriculture, Warsay Yikealo Secondary School, 2018/2019

exam.answer_key_note: No official key exists. All answers were solved independently and checked against the Eritrean MoE Agriculture textbooks Grades 11 and 12 (extracted text with page markers). See confidence and review_flag on each question.

questions.stem: Which of the following is incorrect about agriculture?

options.A: Farming is one of the oldest and the most essential tasks for all
options.B: It is the work which provides us with the basic necessities of our existence
options.C: Farming involves the cultivation of crops and rearing of livestock
options.D: It is not considered as industry

explanation_steps: Statements A, B and C describe agriculture exactly as the textbook introduces it: an old, essential activity that supplies basic necessities through crops and livestock.
Section 4.1.3 'Agriculture as Industry' explains that agriculture is an industry: it uses inputs (land, labour, capital, management) to produce goods for the market, like any other industry.
So the incorrect statement is 'It is not considered as industry'. Answer: D.
tips: 'Incorrect' questions: test every option against the textbook and pick the false one.
Agriculture = an industry that produces food, fibre and raw materials for other (agro-)industries.

similar_questions.stem: Which statement about agriculture is correct?

options.A: Agriculture involves only the growing of crops
options.B: Agriculture is regarded as an industry that combines inputs to produce goods
options.C: Agriculture does not supply raw materials to other industries
options.D: Farming is a recent human activity

explanation_steps: Agriculture includes crops AND livestock (A false); it supplies raw materials such as cotton, hides and milk to agro-industries (C false); it is one of the oldest activities (D false) and a major employer (E false).
The textbook treats agriculture as an industry. Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are roles of soil, except:

options.A: It is medium for plant growth
options.B: It is a source of pollution
options.C: Uses for habitat of soil organism
options.D: It is medium for recycling of nutrients

explanation_steps: The textbook groups the functions of soil into five major ecological roles (Figure 2.2): medium for plant growth, habitat for soil organisms, recycling of nutrients and organic wastes, water supply and purification, and engineering medium (supports buildings and roads).
The textbook says soil FILTERS potential pollutants – it is a purifier, not a source of pollution.
Answer: B.
tips: Remember the five roles: plant growth · habitat for organisms · nutrient recycling · water supply/purification · engineering (building) medium.

similar_questions.stem: Soil removes impurities as water moves down through it. Which role of soil is this?
explanation_steps: As water percolates through soil, particles and microorganisms trap and break down pollutants.
This is the water supply and purification role. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2 Soil (five major ecological roles of soil, Figure 2.2)

questions.stem: Which of the following is a physical soil and water conservation measure?
explanation_steps: Table 3.2 of the textbook lists the physical conservation measures on cropland: terraces, stone bunds, diversion ditches, waterways, gully control and live fencing.
Crop rotation and tillage practices are agronomic practices; afforestation and enclosure are biological measures used on uncultivated hillsides.
Answer: A.
tips: Physical (mechanical) measures are STRUCTURES built with soil/stone: terraces, bunds, ditches, check-dams, waterways.
Biological = plants (afforestation, grass strips, enclosures); agronomic = how the crop is grown (rotation, intercropping, mulching, tillage).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an agronomic (not physical) soil and water conservation practice?
explanation_steps: Stone bunds, terraces, check-dams and diversion ditches are built structures – physical measures.
Intercropping is a cropping practice – agronomic. Answer: C.

questions.stem: One of the following is not concerning importance of a farm manager.

options.B: Keeping records of the farm activity
options.C: Planning and coordinating of the farm activity

explanation_steps: Section 4.1.2 lists the tasks that make a farm manager important: planning and coordinating farm activities, purchasing inputs, keeping records, supervising and paying workers, marketing produce.
Every option A–D is one of those functions, so none of them is 'not concerning' the farm manager.
Answer: E (None of the above).
tips: When each of A–D is a true function, the 'except/not' answer is 'None of the above'.
Management functions: planning → organising/coordinating → implementing → monitoring → evaluation.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of a farm manager?

options.D: Setting the national price of fertilizer

explanation_steps: A farm manager plans production, keeps records, supervises labour and buys inputs.
National input prices are set outside the farm – the manager cannot control them. Answer: D.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most water efficient use method of irrigation?
explanation_steps: The textbook: drip (trickle) irrigation delivers water drop by drop at or near the root zone and 'can be the most water-efficient method of irrigation, if managed properly, since evaporation and runoff are minimized'.
Sprinklers deliver about 75 % of the water to the crop; furrow and basin irrigation only 40–50 %.
Answer: B.
tips: Efficiency order in the textbook: drip > sprinkler (≈75 %) > furrow/basin (40–50 %).
Fertigation = applying fertilizer through drip lines.

similar_questions.stem: About what percentage of the applied water reaches the crop in furrow and basin irrigation, according to the textbook?
explanation_steps: The textbook compares sprinkler irrigation (about 75 % reaches the crop) with 'the common figures of 40–50 per cent in furrow and basin irrigation'.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The detachment and airborne movement of small soil particles caused by the impact of rain drops on the soil is called ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook definition: 'Splash erosion is the detachment and airborne movement of small soil particles caused by the impact of raindrops on soil.'
Sheet erosion removes a thin surface layer by overland sheet flow; rills are small channels; gullies are large, permanent channels; wind erosion is caused by wind.
Answer: A.
tips: Water-erosion sequence: splash (raindrop) → sheet → rill → gully (increasing concentration of flow).

similar_questions.stem: Erosion that forms large channels which are not removed by ordinary tillage is called:
explanation_steps: Rills are small and are smoothed by normal tillage; gullies are deep channels (1–2 m up to 75–150 m) that tillage cannot remove.
Answer: D.

questions.stem: Plants that are grown for feed as hay, silage or pasture are known as ______.
explanation_steps: In the classification of field crops by use, forage crops are crops grown to feed livestock – fed fresh, grazed as pasture or conserved as hay or silage.
Catch (emergence) crops are quick-growing annuals sown after a crop failure; green manure crops are ploughed into the soil; pulses are grain legumes.
Answer: B.
tips: Hay = dried forage; silage = fermented moist forage; soilage = forage cut and fed fresh.

similar_questions.stem: A crop grown and ploughed into the soil while still green to improve soil fertility is a:
explanation_steps: Ploughing in a green crop adds organic matter and nutrients – that is green manuring.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: All of the following are advantages of weeds, except:

options.B: It can be used as manure

explanation_steps: The textbook lists benefits of weeds: a source of animal feed, manure or compost, medicinal value, oil extraction, construction (huts) and soil and water conservation.
Competing with crops for nutrients, water and light is the main HARMFUL effect of weeds.
Answer: D.
tips: Weeds harm crops by competition (nutrients, water, light, space) and by harbouring pests and diseases.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a harmful effect of weeds?

options.A: They are used as animal feed
options.B: They host insect pests and diseases
options.E: They reduce erosion on bare land

explanation_steps: Feed, compost, medicine and erosion control are uses/benefits of weeds.
Harbouring (hosting) pests and diseases is harmful. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Animal feeds can be originated from one of the following, except:
explanation_steps: The textbook's sources of animal feed are natural pastures (grazing land), planted (improved) forages, crop residues (straw, stover) and agro-industrial by-products (brans, oil-seed cakes, molasses).
All of options A–D are sources of feed, so none is an exception.
Answer: E.
tips: Check each option; if all are true in an 'except' question, choose 'None of the above'.

similar_questions.stem: Wheat bran and sesame cake used to feed dairy cows are examples of:
explanation_steps: Bran comes from flour milling and sesame cake from oil extraction – by-products of industries processing crops.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2.2 Common Classifications and Types of Feeds

questions.stem: Tuberculosis can be controlled by ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook's control measures for tuberculosis: good hygiene and sanitation, avoiding overcrowding, and regular testing with isolation/culling of infected (reactor) animals.
Vaccination and proper carcass disposal are described in the same section for other zoonoses (e.g. brucellosis, anthrax) and are general disease-prevention measures in section 1.5.2.
Because A and B are certainly correct and C and D are general control measures, the intended key is 'All of the above'. Answer: E.
tips: TB is a zoonosis spread by milk, meat and breath; test-and-isolate plus hygiene is the basic control.
In 'All of the above' items, make sure at least two options are clearly right.

similar_questions.stem: Which disease of cattle is caused by bacteria and can reach people through raw milk and poorly cooked meat?
explanation_steps: Rabies and FMD are viral; mastitis is an udder infection; Newcastle disease affects poultry.
Bovine tuberculosis is bacterial and transmitted through unpasteurised milk and undercooked meat. Answer: C.

additional_textbook_refs.note: General prevention measures; vaccination for TB is not stated explicitly.

questions.review_flag: Textbook lists hygiene/sanitation, avoiding overcrowding and test-and-isolate for TB; vaccines and carcass disposal are given for brucellosis/other diseases. Key E assumes the setter treats all four as TB controls – teacher should confirm.

questions.stem: The following are the causes for anthropogenic deforestation, except:
explanation_steps: Anthropogenic means caused by human beings.

The textbook's anthropogenic causes: expansion of agricultural area, extraction of wood, overgrazing, unsustainable extraction of non-wood forest products, lack of tree tenure, climate change and recurrent droughts, and consequences of war.
The textbook's natural causes are events such as volcanic eruptions and hurricanes; a landslide is likewise a natural event. Answer: A.
tips: Natural causes (textbook): volcanic eruptions, hurricanes (also landslides). Anthropogenic: farming expansion, wood extraction, overgrazing, war, non-wood product over-extraction.

similar_questions.stem: According to the textbook, which of the following is a NATURAL cause of deforestation?
explanation_steps: Charcoal making, clearing, overgrazing and war are human (anthropogenic) causes.
The textbook names volcanic eruptions and hurricanes as natural causes. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The Eritrean proclamation 156 of 2006 is concerned about ______.

options.C: Promotion of awareness and participation in forest and wildlife management

explanation_steps: Section 2.4.2 (Law Enforcement) lists Eritrean laws on natural resources.
Proclamation No. 156/2006 is the Plant Quarantine Proclamation – it controls the entry and spread of plant pests and diseases.
The forestry and wildlife aims in options A–C (endangered species, afforestation, participation) belong to Proclamation 155 of 2006. Answer: D.
tips: Match each proclamation number with its subject; exam setters like 'Proclamation 156/2006 = plant quarantine'.

similar_questions.stem: The main purpose of plant quarantine is to:

options.B: prevent the introduction and spread of plant pests and diseases

explanation_steps: Quarantine controls the movement of plants and plant products across borders and regions.
Its aim is to stop pests and diseases being introduced or spread. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A good livestock house should not have ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook's requirements for animal houses include warmth/sunlight, good drainage, adequate ventilation and a floor that is easy to clean.
The textbook prefers concrete floors to mud floors, but a SMOOTH concrete floor is slippery – animals slip, fall and are injured – so floors should be roughened or grooved.
The only undesirable feature among the options is therefore the smooth floor. Answer: C.
tips: Good house: dry, well-drained, ventilated, lit, easy to clean, non-slippery floor, protection from weather.

similar_questions.stem: Why should the concrete floor of a cattle house be roughened or grooved?
explanation_steps: A smooth wet floor is slippery; animals can fall and injure legs or udders.
Grooves give grip. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.note: Textbook says concrete floors are more suitable than mud; it does not mention smooth vs rough floors.

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: 'smooth' floors are not discussed (textbook only recommends concrete over mud). Key C relies on the standard rule that floors must be non-slippery.

questions.stem: Which of the following instruments is used for keeping the two jaws of the animal apart when examining the mouth and dosing with oral medicine?
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Gags are instruments used for keeping the two jaws of the animal apart' for mouth examination and oral dosing (e.g. Drinkwater's gag).
Bull holders and nose rings are used to lead and control bulls; a milkman's rope restrains the hind legs during milking.
Answer: D.
tips: Restraint equipment: bull holder/nose ring (head), milkman's rope (hind legs), crush (whole animal), gag (mouth).

similar_questions.stem: Which piece of equipment is used to restrain the hind legs of a cow during milking?
explanation_steps: The milkman's rope is tied around the hind legs to stop kicking during milking.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Water stored in dams can be used for ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook: water from reservoirs is used for human consumption, animal usage and irrigation.
It adds that dams are constructed for water storage for irrigation, hydro-electric power generation, flood control or any combination of these.
All options are uses. Answer: E.
tips: Dams = multipurpose: drinking, livestock, irrigation, hydropower, flood control.

similar_questions.stem: Toker Dam, shown in the Grade 12 textbook, is an example of a structure used for:
explanation_steps: Dams stem the flow of water and store it in reservoirs – a water-harvesting structure.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The plant nutrients that can be supplied from limestone are ______.
explanation_steps: Limestone is calcium carbonate (calcite, CaCO₃); dolomitic limestone also contains magnesium carbonate (dolomite, CaCO₃·MgCO₃) – both named in the textbook.
Liming acid soils therefore supplies calcium and, with dolomitic lime, magnesium.
Answer: C.
tips: Lime corrects soil acidity (raises pH) and adds Ca (and Mg if dolomitic).

similar_questions.stem: Which material is applied to raise the pH of an acid soil?
explanation_steps: Ammonium sulphate, sulphur and urea tend to acidify soil.
Lime (CaCO₃) neutralises acidity. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.11 Chemical Properties of Soil – calcareous and dolomitic soils

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: liming as a Ca/Mg nutrient source is not stated directly; the textbook only gives calcite CaCO₃ and dolomite CaCO₃·MgCO₃. Key C from standard soil chemistry.

questions.stem: Which animal feed is classified as concentrate feed?
explanation_steps: Concentrates are feeds high in energy (or protein) and low in fibre: cereal grains, brans, middlings, oil-seed cakes.
Straw, grasses, hay and stover are bulky, high-fibre roughages.
Answer: D.
tips: Roughage = high fibre, low energy per kg. Concentrate = high energy/protein, low fibre (textbook glossary).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a roughage?
explanation_steps: Grain, bran, cakes and fishmeal are concentrates.
Stover (dry stalks and leaves after grain harvest) is high in fibre – a roughage. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2.2 Common Classifications and Types of Feeds

questions.stem: Which of the following factors is/are not an important factor to increase crop production in Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Fertilizer, improved seed varieties, proper land preparation and timely weeding all raise yields (Unit 3 cultural practices).
The textbook warns that poor and untimely land preparation/planting causes weed problems and yield loss – crops sown late miss the short rainy season.
Untimely planting reduces production. Answer: C.
tips: Timeliness is critical in Eritrea because the rainy season is short and erratic.

similar_questions.stem: Why is timely sowing especially important in Eritrea?

options.B: Because the rainy season is short and unreliable
options.C: Because weeds do not grow early

explanation_steps: Rainfall starts early in the growing season and does not last long (textbook, natural constraints).
Late sowing leaves the crop without enough moisture. Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following is not an aim of cultivation.
explanation_steps: The textbook's aims of cultivation (inter-row tillage of a growing crop): to control weeds, to loosen the soil and improve aeration, to increase infiltration and conserve soil moisture.
Cultivation is meant to REDUCE runoff by improving infiltration, not to increase it.
Answer: C.
tips: More runoff = more erosion and less soil water – never an aim of a good practice.

similar_questions.stem: Breaking a surface crust between crop rows after rain mainly helps to:
explanation_steps: A crust seals the surface; breaking it lets water and air enter the soil.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are roles that livestock play in Eritrea, except:
explanation_steps: Section 1.1.3: livestock plough the land, provide manure, convert crop residues into meat and milk, provide food and income, draught and transport, and 'offer employment opportunities'.
All options A–D are roles of livestock.
Answer: E.
tips: Livestock roles: food · income · draught/transport · manure · employment · savings/insurance · social status.

similar_questions.stem: In Eritrean mixed farming, livestock mainly:

options.A: compete with crops for land only
options.B: plough the land and supply manure

explanation_steps: The textbook: in mixed farming systems livestock are mainly used to plough the land and provide manure for crop fields.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is transmitted to humans through unpasteurized milk and improperly cooked meat?
explanation_steps: The textbook: tuberculosis is transmitted to people by drinking unpasteurised milk and eating improperly cooked meat of infected animals (it is also common in people handling meat).
Brucellosis is described as spread mainly through raw milk and contact with aborted material; rabies by bites; mastitis is an udder disease; anthrax mainly by contact with carcasses/spores.
Only tuberculosis matches BOTH routes in the textbook. Answer: B.
tips: Pasteurisation of milk and thorough cooking of meat prevent milk- and meat-borne zoonoses.

similar_questions.stem: Heating milk to kill disease-causing bacteria without boiling it is called:
explanation_steps: Pasteurisation heats milk to a set temperature for a set time to kill pathogens such as TB and Brucella bacteria.
Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Brucellosis is also milk-borne, so A is partly defensible; key B because the textbook names both unpasteurised milk AND undercooked meat only for TB.

questions.stem: Soil and water conservation is important for the following reasons, except:

options.A: To increase infiltration and reduce runoff water
options.D: To increase speed and extent of soil degradation

explanation_steps: Section 3.1.2 gives the importance of SWC: increasing infiltration and reducing runoff, reducing soil loss, enabling agricultural innovation and intensification, improving productivity.
SWC is meant to SLOW DOWN and reduce soil degradation, not increase it.
Answer: D.
tips: Any option that makes degradation worse cannot be a purpose of conservation.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a benefit of soil and water conservation?

options.C: Reduced soil loss and better infiltration

explanation_steps: Conservation keeps soil and water on the land.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 3.1.2 The Importance of Soil and Water Conservation

questions.stem: Identify the one which is not a type of water erosion.
explanation_steps: The textbook's water erosion types (Table 3.1): splash (raindrop), sheet, rill and gully erosion.
Glacial erosion is caused by moving ICE (the textbook describes it separately as ice erosion), so it is not water erosion.
'Flood erosion' is not a textbook term, but floods are flowing water (sheet floods are part of sheet erosion), so the best answer is B.
tips: Classify erosion by agent: water (splash, sheet, rill, gully), wind (deflation, abrasion), ice (glacial, freeze–thaw).

similar_questions.stem: Deflation and abrasion are effects of:
explanation_steps: The textbook: wind lifts small particles (deflation) and suspended particles strike objects (abrasion).
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.2.3 Soil Erosion – water, ice and wind erosion

questions.review_flag: 'Flood erosion' (A) is also not a textbook term; key B (glacial = ice erosion) is the clearly non-water option.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a fixed cost that does not vary with the level of production?
explanation_steps: Fixed costs do not change with the level of output (e.g. insurance, depreciation, rent, interest, housing of machinery); variable costs rise with output (fuel/oil, repairs, seed, fertilizer).
Insurance is the textbook example of a fixed cost (Grade 12 review questions).
Garage (housing) cost for a machine is also normally fixed, so A and B are both fixed. The intended key is A.
tips: Fixed costs: insurance, depreciation, interest, rent, taxes, housing (garage). Variable: fuel, oil, repairs, labour, seed, fertilizer.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a variable cost for a tractor?
explanation_steps: Insurance, depreciation, interest and garage rent are paid whether or not the tractor works.
Fuel use increases with hours worked. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Two fixed costs among the options: insurance (A) and garage/housing cost (B). Key A (textbook example), B also accepted – teacher decision.

questions.stem: In an agricultural enterprise, which resource is hard to control?
explanation_steps: The textbook separates resources the farm manager can control (land use, labour, capital, seed and other inputs) from factors that are uncontrollable, such as weather.
It states that such factors are 'uncontrollable and the farm manager cannot exercise significant' influence over them – rainfall is the clearest example.
Answer: C.
tips: Weather (rainfall, temperature) = uncontrollable factor; inputs = controllable.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these can a farmer directly control?
explanation_steps: Weather and world prices are beyond the farmer's control.
The rate of fertilizer applied is the farmer's decision. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 4.1.5 Basic Economic Principles – controllable and uncontrollable factors

questions.stem: The soil horizon having limited air and water movement, with soil particles more closely packed, is ______.
explanation_steps: The B-horizon (subsoil) is a zone of illuviation: clay, iron, aluminium and organic matter washed in from above accumulate there (textbook).
Accumulated clay makes the B-horizon denser and more compact, so air and water move slowly through it.
The O-horizon is loose organic litter, the A-horizon is the porous humus-rich topsoil, and the C-horizon is weathered parent material. Answer: B.
tips: Profile from top: O (litter) → A (topsoil) → B (subsoil, accumulation) → C (parent material) → R (bedrock).

similar_questions.stem: The horizon in which humified organic matter is mixed with mineral material near the surface is the:
explanation_steps: The textbook defines the A-horizon as a mineral horizon at or near the surface where humified organic matter is associated with mineral materials.
Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Textbook does not describe compaction/limited air and water movement for any horizon; key B inferred from 'accumulation (illuviation) of clay' in the B-horizon.

questions.stem: All of the following are major soil problems, except:
explanation_steps: The textbook's list of soil problems managed by agronomic practices includes erosion, compaction, swelling and shrinkage (vertisols), acidity and salinity.
Drainage is a SOLUTION (removal of excess water) – poor drainage/waterlogging is the problem.
Answer: C.
tips: Read carefully: 'drainage' (a remedy) vs 'poor drainage' (a problem).

similar_questions.stem: Which practice is used to remove excess water from waterlogged soils?
explanation_steps: Drainage removes excess surface or sub-surface water.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a branch of animal science?
explanation_steps: In the textbook, the divisions of animal science (1.5.2) include animal breeding, animal nutrition, animal physiology, dairy/poultry science and aquaculture.
Agronomy is a division of PLANT science (field crops and soils), and veterinary science is listed under agricultural production support and management (1.5.3), not under animal science.
So both A and D are not branches of animal science. Answer: E.
tips: Plant sciences: agronomy, horticulture, plant breeding, plant protection. Animal sciences: breeding, nutrition, aquaculture, apiculture…

similar_questions.stem: Agronomy deals mainly with:
explanation_steps: Horticulture deals with fruits/vegetables; veterinary science with animal health; aquaculture with fish.
Agronomy = field crop production and soil management. Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following is an incorrect statement about farming systems in Eritrea.

options.A: Mixed farming is the most dominant in Eritrea
options.B: Nomadic pastoralism is also called transhumance
options.C: Nomadic pastoralism is prevalent in the semi-desert area of Eritrea
options.D: Semi-nomadism occurs in the Sheeb area of the Northern Red Sea

explanation_steps: Textbook Table 1.1: sedentary agro-pastoralism (mixed farming) is practised by about 67 % of farmers – the dominant system (A correct).
Nomadic pastoralism is prevalent in the semi-desert agro-ecological zone (C correct); semi-nomadic pastoralism occurs in spate-irrigation areas such as Sheeb (D correct).
Transhumance (seasonal movement between fixed grazing areas) is a form of SEMI-nomadic pastoralism, not of nomadic pastoralism. Answer: B.
tips: Nomadic = no permanent home, continuous movement. Semi-nomadic/transhumance = permanent base + seasonal migration.

similar_questions.stem: Farmers who keep a permanent home and grow some crops but move their herds seasonally to distant grazing areas practise:
explanation_steps: A permanent base plus seasonal migration of herds is transhumance.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The lines connecting locations with the same mean yearly temperature are called ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Isotherms … are the lines connecting the locations with the same mean yearly temperature.'
Isobars join places of equal pressure; contours join points of equal height; isotopes are atoms of the same element with different masses.
Answer: B.
tips: iso = equal; therm = heat; bar = pressure; hyet = rain (isohyet).

similar_questions.stem: Lines on a map joining places with equal rainfall are:
explanation_steps: Isohyets join points of equal rainfall.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following strategies is not used to conserve the indigenous biodiversity in Eritrea?

options.A: Introduce in-situ and ex-situ conservation measures

explanation_steps: Eritrea's biodiversity strategy groups conservation into ten themes including integrated management, sustainable use of natural resources, in-situ and ex-situ conservation and MANAGEMENT of alien invasive species.
Introducing alien invasive species harms indigenous biodiversity – invasive species disrupt the ecological balance (Grade 12, 2.3.3).
Answer: B.
tips: In-situ = conserving in the natural habitat or farmers' fields; ex-situ = in gene banks, zoos, botanical gardens.

similar_questions.stem: Keeping seeds of local crop varieties in a gene bank is an example of:
explanation_steps: Conservation outside the natural habitat (gene bank) is ex-situ.
Answer: B.

additional_textbook_refs.section: 2.3.3 Causes of Wildlife Decline – alien species

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct about river basins in Eritrea?

options.A: Setit River rises in the central part of Eritrea
options.B: Mereb-Gash River rises in central Ethiopia
options.C: Red Sea river flows are used for spate irrigation
options.D: Danakil depression has runoff events of long duration
options.E: Barka-Anseba River has a degree of major soil erosion

explanation_steps: The textbook (2.4.3): 'The Setit River basin rises in central Ethiopia' – so A is wrong, and B wrongly gives the Setit's source to the Mereb-Gash, whose basin forms the southern part of the Central Highlands of Eritrea.
Flows of the Red Sea basin rivers 'are used for spate irrigation and to recharge the shallow coastal aquifers' – C is correct.
Streams of the Danakil basin have runoff events of SHORT duration (D wrong), and it is the upper MEREB-GASH basin that is 'subject to major soil erosion' (E wrong). Answer: C.
tips: Eritrea's basins: Setit, Mereb-Gash, Barka-Anseba (to Sudan), Red Sea, Danakil depression.

similar_questions.stem: Spate irrigation in Eritrea mainly uses:

options.B: short-lived flood flows from seasonal rivers

explanation_steps: Spate irrigation diverts flash floods of seasonal (ephemeral) rivers onto fields, e.g. in Sheeb and the eastern lowlands.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.4.3 The Major River Basins of Eritrea

questions.stem: Suppose fresh alfalfa contains 45% moisture. If a farmer provides 6 kg of fresh alfalfa to a cow daily, how much dry matter per day is the cow obtaining from the alfalfa?
explanation_steps: Dry matter % = 100 % − moisture % = 100 − 45 = 55 %.
Dry matter = 6 kg × 55/100 = 3.3 kg per day.
Answer: B. (2.7 kg is the WATER in the feed: 6 × 0.45.)
tips: Feed = water + dry matter. Always subtract the moisture first.
This is the worked example in the Grade 12 textbook (1.2.1).

similar_questions.stem: Silage contains 70 % moisture. How much dry matter is in 20 kg of this silage?
explanation_steps: Dry matter = 100 − 70 = 30 %.
20 kg × 0.30 = 6 kg. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2.1 Feeds and Feed Composition – water and dry matter

questions.stem: Identify the incorrect statement about dicotyledon plants.

options.A: Has flower parts in multiples of four or five
options.C: Examples are pumpkin, beans and maize

explanation_steps: Textbook Table 3.1: dicots have flower parts in multiples of four or five, roots from the radicle and reticulated leaf veins (A, B, D correct).
The textbook names tomato, beans and pumpkin as dicots, but maize (with barley and sorghum) as a MONOCOT.
Many dicots such as beans and pumpkin show epigeal germination. The incorrect statement is C.
tips: Monocots: cereals (maize, sorghum, barley, wheat, teff) – parallel veins, fibrous roots, flower parts in threes.

similar_questions.stem: Which plant is a monocotyledon?
explanation_steps: Bean, tomato, pumpkin and groundnut are dicots.
Sorghum is a cereal – a monocot. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The crops which are quick-growing annuals sown in the field where crops have failed to produce grain are called ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Catch crops or emergence crops: these are quick-growing' annual crops sown where the main crop has failed.
Cover crops protect the soil surface; soiling crops are cut and fed green; companion crops are grown together with another crop.
Answer: B.
tips: Catch crop = 'catches' the remaining season after failure (also called emergency/emergence crop).

similar_questions.stem: A crop grown mainly to protect bare soil from erosion between main crops is a:
explanation_steps: Protecting the soil surface is the purpose of a cover crop.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of the head-to-head system of intensive dairy cattle housing?

options.A: There is less chance of spreading diseases
options.C: Cows always get more fresh air outside

explanation_steps: The textbook lists advantages of the TAIL-to-tail system: central passage makes cleaning and milking easy, less chance of disease spreading, more fresh air, easy supervision of milking – exactly options A–D.
Advantages of the HEAD-to-head system are different: both rows are fed easily, sunlight falls in the gutter, suitable for narrow barns, cows enter stalls easily.
None of A–D is a head-to-head advantage. Answer: E.
tips: Head-to-head → FEEDING is easy (shared feed alley). Tail-to-tail → MILKING, cleaning and supervision are easy.

similar_questions.stem: Which is an advantage of the head-to-head arrangement of dairy cows?

options.B: Both rows can be fed easily from one alley
options.D: Easier cleaning of the dung channel

explanation_steps: Options A, C, D and E are tail-to-tail advantages.
Head-to-head cows face a common feeding passage. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.4 Animal Housing and Equipment – e) Dairy housing

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a role of wildlife?

options.B: They destroy crop production and livestock
options.C: Used for aesthetic and heritage value

explanation_steps: Section 2.3.1 lists roles (values) of wildlife: food, scientific and educational study, aesthetic and national heritage value, tourism/ecotourism and recreation, ecological balance.
Destroying crops and livestock is a PROBLEM caused by wildlife – the source of human–wildlife conflict (2.3.4), not a role.
Answer: B.
tips: A 'role' is a benefit; damage to crops/livestock is a conflict.

similar_questions.stem: Crop raiding by baboons and predation of goats by hyenas are examples of:
explanation_steps: Damage by wild animals to crops or livestock creates conflict between people and wildlife.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: If a place has a horizontal interval of 80 m and a vertical interval of 20 m, calculate the slope of the place in percent.
explanation_steps: The textbook: percentage slope = (vertical interval ÷ horizontal interval) × 100.
Answer: B. (0.25 is the ratio, not the percentage; 400 is HI/VI × 100.)
tips: Slope % = VI/HI × 100. Ratio form = VI : HI = 1 : 4.

similar_questions.stem: The vertical interval between two points is 6 m and the horizontal interval is 150 m. What is the slope in percent?
explanation_steps: Answer: A.

questions.stem: The protected area in Eritrea for the wild ass is ______.
explanation_steps: Section 2.4.4 lists Eritrea's proposed protected areas.
The Buri Peninsula is the protected area for the African wild ass; Gash-Setit is for elephants, Yob/Nakfa for Nubian ibex, Semenawi Bahri is a forest area.
Answer: C.
tips: The African wild ass is critically endangered; Eritrea (Danakil/Buri) holds one of the last populations.

similar_questions.stem: Which Eritrean area is mainly associated with the conservation of the African elephant?
explanation_steps: Eritrea's elephant population lives in the Gash-Setit area in the south-west.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Why is it important to use surveying techniques and instruments in soil and water conservation?

options.B: It gives guidance on the range of equipment used in simple surveying
options.C: It provides guidance on measuring distances
options.D: For finding differences in height and elevation on maps

explanation_steps: The textbook: surveying techniques are the basis of SWC, tree planting and the layout of structures; the section 'provides guidance on measuring distances, finding differences in height, making and using maps and plans' and describes the equipment used in simple surveying.
Every option restates part of that sentence.
Answer: E.
tips: Surveying in SWC: laying out contours, terraces, bunds; measuring distances, heights and slopes.

similar_questions.stem: Before building contour stone bunds on a hillside, farmers first:

options.B: survey and mark the contour lines

explanation_steps: Bunds must follow the contour, so contour lines are surveyed and pegged first.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The financial statement which reflects the financial position of a farm business on a specific date is known as ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'A balance sheet is a financial statement which reflects the' financial position (assets, liabilities and net worth) of a farm business at a specific date, e.g. the last day of the financial year.
An income statement covers a PERIOD (revenue − expenses = profit); a cash-flow statement records cash in and out over time; assets and liabilities are parts of the balance sheet, not statements.
Answer: B.
tips: Balance sheet = snapshot on one date: Assets = Liabilities + Net worth.
Income statement = film over a period.

similar_questions.stem: On a farm balance sheet, net worth (owner's equity) equals:
explanation_steps: Net worth is what remains to the owner after all debts are subtracted from the assets.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a basic principle of cooperatives?
explanation_steps: The seven co-operative principles in the textbook: voluntary and open membership, democratic member control, member economic participation, autonomy and independence, education/training/information, cooperation among co-operatives, and concern for community.
Membership is VOLUNTARY, so 'involuntary membership' is not a principle.
Answer: B.
tips: Principles begin with 'Voluntary and open membership' – nobody is forced to join.

similar_questions.stem: 'One member, one vote' in a co-operative expresses the principle of:
explanation_steps: Equal voting rights for all members is democratic member control.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 4.4.2 Types of CBO – c) Co-operative principles

questions.stem: The greatest challenges to the conservation of wildlife in Eritrea are ______.
explanation_steps: Section 2.5 (Challenges) discusses three main challenges to forest and wildlife conservation: 2.5.1 Poverty, 2.5.2 Beliefs and 2.5.3 Ownership and Responsibility.
All four options are named challenges.
Answer: E.
tips: Remember the Unit 2 challenges: Poverty · Beliefs · Ownership & responsibility.

similar_questions.stem: Why is poverty a challenge to forest conservation?

options.B: Poor households depend on cutting trees for fuel, income and farmland

explanation_steps: People with few alternatives rely on fuelwood, charcoal sales and clearing land for survival.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which meteorological instrument is used for measuring solar radiation?
explanation_steps: A radiometer (pyranometer/solarimeter) measures the intensity of solar radiation directly – it is the instrument that measures radiation.

The textbook's figure of weather instruments pairs the sunshine recorder with 'sunshine (daylight) hours and intensity'; a rain gauge measures rainfall, a barometer air pressure, a thermo-hygrograph temperature and humidity.
Key D (radiometer); C (sunshine recorder) is accepted because the textbook links it to sunshine intensity.
tips: Sunshine recorder (Campbell–Stokes) = hours of bright sunshine. Radiometer/pyranometer = amount (energy) of radiation.

similar_questions.stem: Which instrument measures atmospheric pressure?
explanation_steps: Anemometer – wind speed; rain gauge – rainfall; hygrometer – humidity; evaporation pan – evaporation.
Barometer (barograph) – pressure. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.note: Textbook figure shows a sunshine recorder (sunshine hours and intensity) but no radiometer.

questions.review_flag: Radiometer is not in the textbook; the textbook's instrument figure only has a sunshine recorder (C). Key D, C also accepted – teacher decision.

questions.stem: Which of the following groups of plant nutrients is not a group of trace nutrients?
explanation_steps: The textbook: micronutrients (trace elements) are seven elements – manganese, iron, molybdenum, copper, boron, zinc and chlorine.
Sulphur is a secondary MACRO-nutrient (with calcium and magnesium), so group B is not entirely trace nutrients.
Answer: B.
tips: Mnemonic for the 7 micronutrients: 'Mn Fe Mo Cu B Zn Cl'.
Macronutrients: N, P, K (primary); Ca, Mg, S (secondary) + C, H, O.

similar_questions.stem: Which nutrient is a macronutrient?
explanation_steps: Zn, B, Mo and Cu are micronutrients.
Magnesium is a secondary macronutrient. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Identify the correct characteristic of co-operatives.

options.A: They have not an economic purpose
options.B: They are not owned and controlled by the members
options.C: They are not run for the benefit of their members
options.D: They are not charities or state-directed organizations

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Generally, co-operatives have an economic purpose, are owned and controlled by the members, are run for the benefit of members, and are not charities or state-directed organizations.'
Options A–C contradict the first three parts of the sentence; D repeats the last part.
Answer: D.
tips: Watch the negatives: only one option keeps the 'not' in the right place.

similar_questions.stem: A co-operative is best described as:

options.B: an autonomous association of people united voluntarily to meet common economic, social and cultural needs
options.D: a private company owned by one person
options.E: a bank owned by the state

explanation_steps: The textbook definition: an autonomous association of persons united voluntarily to meet common objectives through a jointly owned and democratically controlled enterprise.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cause of wildlife decline in Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Textbook 2.3.3 lists the causes of wildlife decline: habitat destruction and fragmentation, recurrent droughts, unsustainable illegal wildlife trade, Holocene mass extinction, hunting and overkill, war, alien species, cultural beliefs, chain of extinction.
Every option is on the list.
Answer: E.
tips: Habitat destruction is the most important cause worldwide.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these is NOT listed in the textbook as a cause of wildlife decline?
explanation_steps: Protected areas are a conservation effort (2.4.4), not a cause of decline.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is physical soil degradation?
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Physical soil degradation: deterioration of soil structure is a common form of physical degradation in Eritrea'. Erosion is its major cause.
Loss of nutrients, salinization and element imbalance are CHEMICAL degradation; reduction of soil organisms is BIOLOGICAL degradation.
Answer: A.
tips: Types of land degradation: physical (structure, compaction, erosion), chemical (nutrient loss, salinity, acidity, toxicity), biological (loss of organic matter/organisms).

similar_questions.stem: Salinization of irrigated land is an example of:
explanation_steps: Accumulation of salts changes the soil's chemistry.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following livestock is not in the order Perissodactyla.
explanation_steps: Perissodactyla are odd-toed hoofed animals (horses, donkeys, zebras, rhinos) – the textbook places horses in this order.
Cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and camels are even-toed ungulates (Artiodactyla).
So cattle, pigs and sheep are all not Perissodactyla – 'all except B (horse)'. Answer: E.
tips: Peri-SSO = odd (1 or 3 toes: horse, donkey). ARTIO = even (2 or 4 toes: cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, camels).

similar_questions.stem: Which farm animal belongs to the order Artiodactyla (even-toed ungulates)?
explanation_steps: Horse, donkey, mule and zebra are odd-toed (Perissodactyla).
Goats have two main toes – even-toed. Answer: D.

textbook_ref.note: The textbook sentence on p.4 mixes up the 'even/odd-toed' wording, but it clearly places horses in Perissodactyla and camels/cattle among the even-toed animals.

questions.review_flag: Textbook p.4 contains a wording error about even/odd toes; the key follows standard zoology (Perissodactyla = odd-toed: horse).

questions.stem: The ratio of total physical product to the quantity of input is called ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Average product (AP) is the ratio of TP to the quantity of input used in producing that amount of product.' APP = TPP ÷ X.
Marginal physical product is the CHANGE in TPP per extra unit of input (ΔTPP ÷ ΔX).
Answer: A.
tips: APP = TPP/X (average). MPP = ΔTPP/ΔX (extra output from one more unit).

similar_questions.stem: If 4 kg of fertilizer gives a total product of 20 quintals, the average physical product is:
explanation_steps: APP = TPP ÷ input = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 quintals per kg.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Suppose the cost price of a milking machine is 10,000 Nakfa and its salvage value is 5,000 Nakfa after a lifetime of 5 years. Calculate the annual depreciation and the book value at the end of year 2, respectively.
explanation_steps: Textbook formula (straight-line): annual depreciation = (CP − SV) ÷ E.
Depreciation = (10,000 − 5,000) ÷ 5 = 5,000 ÷ 5 = 1,000 Nakfa per year.
Book value after 2 years = 10,000 − 2 × 1,000 = 8,000 Nakfa.
Answer: B (1000 and 8000).
tips: Book value at end of year n = CP − n × annual depreciation. It never falls below the salvage value.

similar_questions.stem: A water pump costs 24,000 Nakfa, has a salvage value of 4,000 Nakfa and a life of 10 years. What is its book value at the end of year 3?
explanation_steps: Annual depreciation = (24,000 − 4,000) ÷ 10 = 2,000 Nakfa.
Book value = 24,000 − 3 × 2,000 = 18,000 Nakfa. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Poor soil drainage is not caused when ______.

options.A: Soils with high clay content impede the movement of surface water
options.C: Hard pans in clay content are found in the subsoil
options.D: Too much rainfall falls during the rainy season

explanation_steps: The textbook: poor soil drainage is caused when too much rainfall is received, soils with high clay content impede drainage, permeable sand/gravel lies over an impermeable clay layer, and hard pans are found in the subsoil.
Compaction also closes pores and slows drainage.
A well-aerated soil has many large pores through which water drains freely – it is not a cause of poor drainage. Answer: B.
tips: Aeration and drainage go together: waterlogged soil = no air in the pores.

similar_questions.stem: Which soil condition is most likely to lead to waterlogging?

options.C: Clay soil over an impermeable hardpan

explanation_steps: Clay and a hardpan both slow downward movement of water.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a factor of production in agriculture?
explanation_steps: The textbook's factors of production in agriculture: land, labour, capital, management and entrepreneurship.
Goods and services are the OUTPUTS produced by combining these factors.
Answer: C.
tips: Inputs (factors): land, labour, capital, management/entrepreneurship. Outputs: goods and services.

similar_questions.stem: Tractors, buildings and irrigation equipment are classified as which factor of production?
explanation_steps: The textbook: everything used in production that is not a gift of nature but made by people is capital (fixed capital).
Answer: C.

questions.stem: There is always conflict between humans and wildlife. To solve the problem, which of the following pieces of information is it important to gather?
explanation_steps: The textbook analyses human–wildlife conflict with the DPSIR framework: Driving forces – Pressures – State of the environment – Impacts – Responses.
Information on the driving forces, pressures, state and impacts is all needed before choosing the responses.
Answer: E.
tips: DPSIR: Driving forces (human activities) → Pressures (e.g. habitat loss) → State (e.g. land degradation) → Impacts → Responses (solutions).

similar_questions.stem: In the DPSIR framework, loss of wildlife habitat caused by farm expansion is an example of:
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Pressure means human activities that result in some sort of pressure on the environment. Loss of habitat … is an example of such pressure.'
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The branch of horticulture that deals with fruits is called ______.
explanation_steps: Textbook branches of horticulture: pomology – fruit crops (e.g. banana, apples); olericulture – vegetables; floriculture – flowers; landscape/ornamental horticulture – beautifying surroundings.
Answer: A.
tips: Pom- (Latin pomum = fruit/apple); oleri- = vegetables; flori- = flowers.

similar_questions.stem: The production of lettuce, cabbage and tomatoes belongs to:
explanation_steps: Vegetable production = olericulture.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Identify the farm animal which has the lowest fat percentage in its milk.
explanation_steps: The textbooks do not give milk composition for different species, so standard dairy-science values are used.
Typical milk fat: sheep ≈ 6–7 %, sow (pig) ≈ 7–8 %, goat ≈ 4–4.5 %, cow ≈ 3.5–4 % (zebu higher), dromedary camel ≈ 2.9–4 % (varies widely with feed and water).
Camel milk is usually quoted as the lowest in fat of these. Key: A.
tips: High-fat milks: sheep and pig; medium: goat and cow; camel milk is lower in fat and rich in vitamin C.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these animals produces milk with the HIGHEST fat percentage?
explanation_steps: Sheep milk has about 6–7 % fat, higher than goat (~4 %), cow (~4 %), camel (~3 %) or donkey (~1 %).
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3 Routine Management Practices – dairy breeds and milk fat
textbook_ref.note: The textbook mentions breed differences in fat content (e.g. Jersey) but gives no species comparison.

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: species milk-fat values are not in the Grade 11/12 textbooks, and published camel and cow values overlap. Key A (camel) from standard tables – teacher should confirm the intended answer.

questions.stem: If a farmer puts 5000 seeds in a germination test and 3000 seeds germinate, find the germination percentage.
explanation_steps: Textbook formula: germination percent = (G1 ÷ G2) × 100, where G1 = germinated seeds and G2 = total seeds tested.
Answer: B. (0.6 is the fraction, not the percentage.)
tips: Always multiply the fraction by 100 when a percentage is asked.

similar_questions.stem: Of 400 wheat seeds tested, 340 germinated. What is the germination percentage?
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: The cheapest and best method of insect control in crop production is ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The use of insect-resistant varieties is the cheapest and best method of insect control in crop plants.' Resistant varieties also give higher and better-quality yields.
Answer: A.
tips: Resistant varieties need no extra cost at the time of the pest attack – the protection is in the seed.

similar_questions.stem: Using ladybird beetles to control aphids is an example of:
explanation_steps: Using a natural enemy (predator) against a pest is biological control.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.3.6 Weeds, Insects and Diseases – insect control

questions.stem: What are the objectives of enclosures?

options.A: To create favourable growth conditions for vegetation
options.B: To protect local flora and fauna from extinction
options.C: To reduce soil erosion and avoid siltation

explanation_steps: The textbook's objectives of enclosures: create favourable growth conditions for vegetation recovery by natural regeneration; reserve pastures for livestock and wood biomass; protect local flora and fauna from local extinction; reduce runoff and increase infiltration; improve groundwater recharge; reduce soil erosion and avoid siltation of dams.
All options are listed. Answer: E.
tips: Enclosure = an area protected (fully or partly) from grazing and cutting so that natural vegetation regenerates.

similar_questions.stem: Enclosures in Eritrea are usually established on:

options.B: steep, severely degraded slopes away from settlements

explanation_steps: The textbook: enclosures are usually located on steep slopes, on severely eroded and degraded land, distant from settlements.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are ectoparasites, except:
explanation_steps: The textbook: parasites that live on the surface of the host are ectoparasites (flies, fleas, ticks, mites, lice).
Endoparasites live inside the body: roundworms, tapeworms, FLUKES (e.g. liver fluke) and protozoa.
Answer: B.
tips: Ecto = outside (skin); endo = inside (gut, liver, blood).

similar_questions.stem: Liver fluke in sheep is an example of:
explanation_steps: It lives inside the bile ducts of the liver.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is different from the others based on the type of industry that produces it?
explanation_steps: Agriculture supplies raw materials to agro-industries such as food-processing, textile and leather industries (G11 1.2.4).
Shoes, bags, wallets and (leather) jackets are products of the leather industry, made from hides and skins.
Yogurt is made from milk by the food-processing (dairy) industry. Answer: B.
tips: Group products by raw material: hides/skins → leather goods; milk → cheese, butter, yogurt; cotton/wool → textiles.

similar_questions.stem: Which product is made by the same agro-industry as cheese?
explanation_steps: Cheese and butter are both dairy (milk-processing) products.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following practices helps to improve the genetic make-up of animals?
explanation_steps: The textbook distinguishes improving the ENVIRONMENT (feeding, housing, disease control, management) from improving the GENETIC make-up (breeding: selection and cross-breeding).
Artificial insemination introduces the semen of a high-quality sire into local females – a cross-breeding method that changes the genes of the offspring.
Options A, B, D and E improve the environment only. Answer: C.
tips: Genetic improvement = selection, culling, cross-breeding (natural service or AI). Environment = feed, health, housing, management.

similar_questions.stem: Which practice improves the environment rather than the genetics of animals?

options.E: Culling of poor producers from breeding

explanation_steps: Selection, cross-breeding, AI and culling change which genes are passed on.
Feeding improves the environment. Answer: D.

questions.stem: A practice of growing a succession of different crops over the years on the same piece of land is called ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Crop rotation is a system of land-use practice in which crops are grown in sequence on the same piece of land.'
Intercropping and mixed cropping grow crops at the SAME time; fallowing leaves land uncultivated; mono-cropping grows one crop repeatedly.
Answer: D.
tips: Rotation = different crops one AFTER another; intercropping = different crops TOGETHER.

similar_questions.stem: Growing sorghum and beans together in alternate rows in the same season is:
explanation_steps: Two crops grown together in a definite row pattern = intercropping.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a digestive organ in poultry?
explanation_steps: The textbook: the poultry digestive system comprises the mouth, crop, proventriculus (glandular stomach), gizzard, small intestine, two caeca, large intestine and cloaca.
The rumen is the fermentation compartment of the stomach of ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats).
Answer: B.
tips: Birds grind food in the gizzard (with grit) because they have no teeth.

similar_questions.stem: In chickens, food is stored and softened before digestion in the:
explanation_steps: The crop is a pouch of the oesophagus that stores and moistens food.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.4 Types and Classification of Livestock – digestive systems

questions.stem: One of the following is not a common method of identification in livestock.
explanation_steps: Textbook methods of identifying livestock: tattooing, tagging, ear-notching and branding.
Castration is the removal/destruction of the testes to make males docile and improve meat – it is not identification.
Answer: C.
tips: Identification purposes: identifying animals, certification, accurate record keeping.

similar_questions.stem: Fixing numbers or letters on the skin of cattle with a hot iron or chemicals is called:
explanation_steps: The textbook defines branding this way; it suits cattle, buffalo, horses and camels.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3 Routine Management Practices – j) Methods used to identify livestock

questions.stem: If an adult castrated male goat is called a wither, then an adult uncastrated male goat is called ______.
explanation_steps: Textbook glossary: buck – adult uncastrated male goat; doe – adult female goat; wither (wether) – adult castrated male goat.
Ram and ewe are the male and female of SHEEP; gimmer refers to sheep.
Answer: A.
tips: Goat: buck (male), doe (female), kid (young), wether (castrated male). Sheep: ram, ewe, lamb.

similar_questions.stem: An adult female goat is called a:
explanation_steps: Ewe = female sheep; heifer = young female cattle.
Doe = adult female goat. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an advantage of bare-root seedlings?

options.A: Less complicated to grow in the nursery
options.B: Roots are not exposed to air drying during lifting and transplanting
options.D: Well suited to large nurseries for economical seed production

explanation_steps: Textbook advantages of bare-root seedlings: less complicated to grow, lighter to transport, suited to mechanisation and to large centralized nurseries, cheaper to produce than potted seedlings.
Bare-root seedlings have NO soil around the roots, so their roots ARE exposed to drying during lifting and transplanting – protection of roots is an advantage of containerized (potted) seedlings.
Answer: B.
tips: Potted seedlings: higher survival on difficult sites, but heavy and expensive. Bare-root: cheap and light, but roots dry out easily.

similar_questions.stem: Which is an advantage of containerized (potted) seedlings over bare-root seedlings?

options.C: Higher survival rate when planted on difficult sites

explanation_steps: Options A, B, D and E are bare-root advantages.
The textbook: potted seedlings have a higher survival rate on difficult sites. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.6 Seedling Planting – a) containerized and b) bare-root seedlings

questions.stem: The interaction between crops and weeds for the available resources is called ______.
explanation_steps: Weeds and crops struggle for the same limited resources – nutrients, water, light and space. The textbook calls this competition (e.g. severe competition lowers yields; competition for light).
Mutualism benefits both, commensalism benefits one without harming the other, neutralism has no effect.
Answer: C.
tips: Weed competition is most harmful early in crop growth – weed early.

similar_questions.stem: Two plant species living together where both benefit (e.g. legume and Rhizobium) show:
explanation_steps: The legume gets nitrogen and the bacteria get carbohydrates – both benefit.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: The book which records only cash transactions is known as ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'A petty cash book (i.e. a book in which only cash transactions are recorded) should be used' for small cash payments.
A wage book records labour and wages; a journal and cash-analysis book record all transactions including cheques.
Answer: B.
tips: Payments by cheque go in the chequebook counterfoils; small cash payments go in the petty cash book.

similar_questions.stem: Details of labourers employed and wages paid are recorded in the:
explanation_steps: Labour records (names, days worked, wages) are kept in the wage book.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the tangible roles of forests is production of wood and non-wood forest products. Which of the following is a wood forest product?
explanation_steps: The textbook lists non-wood (non-timber) forest products: herbal medicine, fibres, gums and resins, wild fruits, honey and wild vegetables. Incense (frankincense) is a resin.
Charcoal is made by burning WOOD – it is a wood product, like firewood, poles and timber.
Answer: D.
tips: Wood products: timber, poles, firewood, charcoal. Non-wood: gums, resins, incense, fruits, honey, medicine, fibres.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a non-wood forest product?
explanation_steps: Timber, fuelwood, poles and charcoal come from wood.
Honey is a non-wood product. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.3 The Role of Forests – b) Tangible uses

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a factor of the speed and extent of soil degradation?
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The speed and extent of soil degradation depends on different factors, such as types of soils, relief, climate and the intensity of land use.'
All four options are factors. Answer: E.
tips: Four factors: soil type · relief · climate · intensity of land use.

similar_questions.stem: Why do the Eritrean Highlands suffer the most land degradation?

options.B: They have steep relief and the greatest livestock and land-use pressure

explanation_steps: The textbook: the Highlands have the greatest livestock density and major degradation; steep slopes speed up erosion.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are beef cattle breeds, except:
explanation_steps: Textbook beef breeds: Angus, Hereford, Simmental, Charolais, Limousin, Gelbvieh, Brahman and Shorthorn.
Guernsey is listed with the DAIRY breeds (Holstein-Friesian, Jersey, Guernsey, Brown Swiss, Ayrshire, Milking Shorthorn).
Answer: B.
tips: Dairy breeds are angular with large udders; beef breeds are block-like.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a dairy breed?
explanation_steps: Hereford, Angus, Charolais and Limousin are beef breeds.
Jersey is a dairy breed. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a yield-defining factor that constrains agricultural development?
explanation_steps: Textbook: yield-defining factors (cannot be changed much at farm level) are CO₂ concentration, solar radiation, temperature, atmospheric humidity, crop physiology, altitude and latitude, species/breeds/crop types.
Yield-LIMITING factors are water and plant nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus (and potassium) – the farmer can supply them.
Answer: B.
tips: Defining = fixed by nature (climate, altitude, crop type). Limiting = water and nutrients (can be added). Reducing = weeds, pests, diseases.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a yield-limiting factor?
explanation_steps: Latitude, physiology, radiation and altitude are yield-defining.
Water is yield-limiting. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an example of a chemical property of soil?
explanation_steps: The textbook lists soil consistency among the PHYSICAL properties (with texture, structure, the liquid and gaseous phases, temperature, depth, colour); it describes resistance of soil to deformation.
Soil pH, colloids, ion (cation) exchange and salinity are treated under 2.2.11 Chemical Properties of Soil.
Answer: C.
tips: Physical: texture, structure, consistency, colour, water, air, temperature. Chemical: pH, colloids, CEC, salinity/sodicity, nutrients.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these is a physical property of soil?
explanation_steps: pH, CEC, salinity and nutrients are chemical properties.
Texture (sand/silt/clay proportions) is physical. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The factors that affect soil formation are ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook: soil is formed 'as a function of the following soil-forming factors: parent material, climate, biota and topography acting over time'.
All options are soil-forming factors. Answer: E.
tips: Five soil-forming factors: ClORPT – Climate, Organisms (biota), Relief (topography), Parent material, Time.

similar_questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the five soil-forming factors?
explanation_steps: The five factors are parent material, climate, organisms, topography and time.
Fertilizer is a management input. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which agro-ecological zone in Eritrea receives the lowest amount of rainfall annually?
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 2.13 gives annual rainfall: sub-humid 700–1100 mm, arid highland 200–500 mm, moist highland 500–700 mm, moist lowland 500–800 mm, arid lowland 200–500 mm, semi-desert < 200 mm.
The semi-desert (coastal area, islands, north-west of the Barka) has the lowest rainfall.
Answer: D.
tips: Semi-desert = largest zone (39 % of the area) and driest (< 200 mm); sub-humid = smallest (1 %) and wettest.

similar_questions.stem: Which agro-ecological zone of Eritrea covers the largest area?
explanation_steps: Table 2.13: semi-desert 48,772 km² (39 %), arid lowland 34 %, moist lowland 16 %, moist highland 7 %, arid highland 3 %, sub-humid 1 %.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: One of the following crops is a long-day plant that needs a photoperiod greater than 12 hours.
explanation_steps: The textbook: long-day plants develop and produce normally when the photoperiod is greater than 12 hours; short-day plants need less than 12 hours; day-neutral plants are unaffected.
Wheat (like barley and oats – temperate cereals) is a classic long-day plant.
Maize and tobacco are generally short-day (or day-neutral) plants; tomato and most beans are day-neutral. Answer: C.
tips: Temperate crops (wheat, barley, oats, temperate onion varieties) → long-day. Tropical crops (maize, sorghum, rice, soybean) → short-day.

similar_questions.stem: Which crop is a typical short-day plant?
explanation_steps: Wheat, barley, oats and temperate onion varieties are long-day plants.
Sorghum (a tropical cereal) is short-day. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of propagation by seeds?

options.A: It is easy to use machines for planting
options.B: It presents a high degree of viability
options.C: Seeds are easier to handle and convenient to transport
options.D: They are easier to store than cuttings

explanation_steps: Propagation by seed is compared with vegetative propagation in section 3.5.6.

Standard advantages of seed propagation: seeds can be sown by machine, are small, light and easy to handle and transport, can be stored for long periods (better than cuttings), and good seed lots have high viability (germination).
Each option is an advantage, so the key is E.
tips: Seed propagation: cheap, easy, storable, mechanisable, but offspring vary genetically. Vegetative: true-to-type, but bulky material that stores poorly.

similar_questions.stem: Which is an advantage of vegetative propagation over seed propagation?

options.A: Planting material is easy to store for years
options.B: Offspring are identical (true to type) to the parent plant
options.C: It is easy to sow by machine
options.D: Planting material is light to transport

explanation_steps: Storage, machine sowing and light weight are advantages of seed.
Vegetative propagation produces clones identical to the parent. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.note: The textbook asks for advantages of vegetative vs seed propagation but does not list them.

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: advantages of seed propagation are not listed; option B ('high degree of viability') is loosely worded. Key E from standard horticulture.

questions.stem: Which of the following feedstuffs are the most highly concentrated sources of energy for animals?
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Lipids are a highly concentrated source of energy. Oxidation of lipids results in 2.25 times more energy than carbohydrate on a unit weight basis.'
Carbohydrates are the MAIN (cheapest, most used) energy source, but fats are the most CONCENTRATED. Vitamins and minerals supply no energy.
Answer: A.
tips: 'Main' energy source → carbohydrates; 'most concentrated' energy source → fats (2.25 ×).

similar_questions.stem: Fats supply about how many times more energy than the same weight of carbohydrates?
explanation_steps: The textbook gives 2.25 times.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: The system of feeding in which forage is cut and taken to the animal is called ______.
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Zero grazing (cut-and-carry method)': forage is cut and carried to animals kept in a stall or pen.
Strip, rotational and deferred grazing and tethering all let the animal graze in the field.
Answer: A. (The same item appears as Review Question 12 of Unit One.)
tips: Zero grazing suits dairy cows in peri-urban areas – less energy wasted walking, manure is collected.

similar_questions.stem: Tying an animal with a rope to a peg so that it grazes only within a circle is called:
explanation_steps: Grazing restricted by a rope and peg = tethering.
Answer: B.

questions.stem:
A saturated soil sample has a mass of 100 g and an oven-dry mass of 80 g, and its total volume is 40 cm³. Calculate: (4 points)
A) Bulk density in g/cm³   B) Porosity   C) Particle density in g/cm³   D) Water content in percentage
questions.answer: A) Bulk density = 80 g ÷ 40 cm³ = 2.0 g/cm³. B) Porosity = 20 cm³ ÷ 40 cm³ = 0.5 = 50 %. C) Particle density = 80 g ÷ 20 cm³ = 4.0 g/cm³. D) Water content = (100 − 80) ÷ 100 × 100 = 20 % (textbook formula, wet-mass basis); on a dry-mass basis 20 ÷ 80 × 100 = 25 %.

subparts.label: D
subparts.question: Water content (%)
subparts.answer: 20 % (wet basis, textbook formula); 25 % on a dry basis

explanation_steps: Mass of water = saturated mass − oven-dry mass = 100 − 80 = 20 g. Density of water = 1 g/cm³, so the water occupies 20 cm³.
In a SATURATED soil all pores are full of water, so pore volume = water volume = 20 cm³ and volume of solids = 40 − 20 = 20 cm³.
A) Bulk density = oven-dry mass ÷ total volume = 80 ÷ 40 = 2.0 g/cm³ (textbook: weight of oven-dry soil ÷ total volume).
B) Porosity f = volume of pores ÷ total volume = 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5 → 50 %.
C) Particle density = oven-dry mass ÷ volume of solids only = 80 ÷ 20 = 4.0 g/cm³.
D) Textbook (gravimetric method): WC % = [(W1 − W2) ÷ W1] × 100 = (100 − 80) ÷ 100 × 100 = 20 %. Many soil books use the dry basis: 20 ÷ 80 × 100 = 25 %.
marking_points: Bulk density = 80/40 = 2.0 g/cm³ (1)
Particle density = 80/20 = 4.0 g/cm³ (1)
Water content = 20 % using the textbook formula (W1 − W2)/W1 × 100; accept 25 % if the dry-mass basis is shown (1)
tips: Check: porosity = 1 − (bulk density ÷ particle density) = 1 − 2.0/4.0 = 0.5 ✓.
Real mineral soils have particle density ≈ 2.65 g/cm³ and bulk density 1.1–1.6 g/cm³ – the numbers in this question are artificial.
Write the formula, substitute, and give units (g/cm³ or %) – each part is worth 1 point.

similar_questions.stem: A saturated soil core of total volume 50 cm³ weighs 90 g; after oven drying it weighs 70 g. Find the bulk density, porosity and particle density.
similar_questions.answer: Water = 20 g = 20 cm³ (= pore volume). Bulk density = 70 ÷ 50 = 1.4 g/cm³. Porosity = 20 ÷ 50 = 40 %. Solids = 50 − 20 = 30 cm³, particle density = 70 ÷ 30 ≈ 2.33 g/cm³.
explanation_steps: Saturated → pores are full of water, so water volume = pore volume.
