questions.stem:
There are several routine management jobs in animal farms. Define the following routine management practices in livestock: (4 points)
A) Culling   B) Docking   C) Branding   D) Shearing
questions.answer: A) Culling – removing (selling or slaughtering) animals with undesirable characteristics, e.g. low milk yield, poor fertility, disease or old age, from the herd/flock. B) Docking – cutting off (shortening) the tail of young animals such as lambs or piglets, for hygiene (prevents dirt and fly strike around the tail) and to ease mating/handling. C) Branding – marking an animal for identification by fixing numbers, letters or designs on the skin with a hot iron or chemicals. D) Shearing – clipping/cutting off the wool (fleece) or hair of sheep (and some goats) for use and to keep the animal clean and cool.
explanation_steps: Culling: the textbook defines it as 'the practice of removing animals with undesirable characteristics or traits' (examples: low milk production, uneconomic type, low birth/weaning weight, poor disease resistance).
Branding: the textbook – fixing numbers, letters, designs or a combination on the skin with a hot iron or chemicals; suited to cattle, buffalo, horses and camels; calves branded at about one year.
Docking and shearing are standard routine practices (sheep and pigs) that are not described in the textbook; the definitions follow standard animal husbandry.
marking_points: Culling: removal of animals with undesirable traits (low production, disease, old age) (1)
Docking: cutting/shortening the tail of lambs, piglets etc. (1)
Branding: permanent identification marks on the skin using a hot iron or chemicals (1)
Shearing: cutting/clipping wool (fleece) or hair from sheep/goats (1)
tips: One clear sentence per term with the key idea: culling = remove; docking = tail; branding = hot-iron/chemical marks for identification; shearing = wool removal.
Other routine practices in the textbook: dehorning, castration, hoof trimming, identification (tattooing, tagging, ear-notching).

similar_questions.stem: Define dehorning and castration and give one reason for each.
similar_questions.answer: Dehorning – removal of an animal's horns (or horn buds) to prevent it from injuring other animals and handlers and to avoid bruised carcasses. Castration – removal or destruction of the testicles of a male animal to make it docile and easier to handle, prevent unwanted breeding and improve meat quality.
explanation_steps: Both are described in the Grade 12 textbook under routine management practices (1.3).

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: docking and shearing are not defined in the Grade 11/12 textbooks; model answers use standard animal-husbandry definitions.

questions.stem: Mention any four advantages of drainage. (2 points)
questions.answer: Any four: (1) increases soil aeration (air returns to the pores, roots can breathe); (2) increases the root zone – roots grow deeper and spread out; (3) raises soil temperature, which speeds up chemical reactions so plants can absorb nutrients; (4) increases the activity of beneficial soil micro-organisms; also: removes excess salts from irrigated land (controls salinity), prevents waterlogging damage to crops/fruit trees, and makes cultivation easier and earlier.
explanation_steps: The textbook (3.5.5) lists the advantages of drainage: increase in soil aeration; increase in the root zone of plants; higher soil temperature so plants absorb plant food because chemical reactions between mineral elements are encouraged; increased activity of micro-organisms.
It also explains that drainage removes temporary excesses of water (preventing damage to crops) and, with periodic flushing, controls salinity in irrigated fields.
marking_points: Increases soil aeration (½)
Increases/deepens the root zone (½)
Warms the soil → better nutrient uptake/chemical reactions (½)
Increases micro-organism activity (½)
Also accept: controls salinity, prevents waterlogging damage, easier/earlier cultivation
tips: Four correct points × ½ point = 2 points. Use the textbook's four points first.

similar_questions.stem: Give three problems caused by poorly drained (waterlogged) soils.
similar_questions.answer: Roots suffocate because air is driven out of the pores; toxic materials accumulate and micro-organism activity falls; soil is difficult to cultivate and becomes compacted and cold; fertility is low, giving stunted, patchy plants.
explanation_steps: Textbook 3.5.4: poorly drained soils are not suitable for crops – toxic materials accumulate, roots are inhibited, cultivation destroys structure and fertility is very low.

questions.stem:
Answer question 4 based on Table 1 (hypothetical production function of wheat). (4 points)
A) Find the APP at 2 kg/ha fertilizer level.
B) Find the MPP at 5 kg/ha fertilizer level.
C) Find the price per unit of wheat product in Nakfa.
D) At which level of fertilizer is the profit-maximizing input level found?

stem_tables.title: Table 1: Hypothetical production function of wheat (as printed)
columns: Marginal value product, MVP (printed unit: kg/ha)
stem_tables.note: Blank cells are to be worked out by the student. The MVP column is labelled '(Kg/ha)' in the paper (as in textbook Table 4.3); MVP is really in Nakfa.

questions.answer: A) APP = TPP ÷ X = 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 kg of wheat per kg of fertilizer. B) MPP = ΔTPP ÷ ΔX = (9 − 8) ÷ (5 − 4) = 1 kg. C) MVP = MPP × price of product; at 2 kg/ha MPP = 5 − 2 = 3 and MVP = 9, so price = 9 ÷ 3 = 3 Nakfa per kg (check at 6 kg: −6 ÷ −2 = 3). D) Profit is maximized where MVP = price of the input (6 Nkf): at 3 kg/ha, MVP = 2 × 3 = 6 Nkf. So the profit-maximizing level is 3 kg/ha of fertilizer.
explanation_steps: Textbook formulas: AP = y/x (Equation 4.4); MP = change in total product ÷ change in input (Equation 4.5); MVP = MP × Po (Equation 4.6).
A) APP at 2 kg/ha = 5/2 = 2.5 kg/kg.
B) MPP at 5 kg/ha = (9 − 8)/(5 − 4) = 1 kg/kg.
C) At 2 kg/ha: MPP = (5 − 2)/(2 − 1) = 3; MVP = 9 = 3 × Po → Po = 3 Nakfa. Check at 6 kg/ha: MPP = 7 − 9 = −2, MVP = −2 × 3 = −6 ✓.
Full MVP column (MPP × 3): 3, 9, 6, 3, 3, −6 for levels 1–6.

D) Textbook rule: 'The profit maximizing input level is at the point where the marginal value product equals the price of the input.' MVP = 6 = Pi at 3 kg/ha; beyond that MVP (3) < 6, so extra fertilizer loses money. Answer: 3 kg/ha.
marking_points: Price of wheat = MVP/MPP = 9/3 = 3 Nkf (1)
Profit-maximizing level 3 kg/ha where MVP = input price = 6 Nkf (1)
tips: If MVP > input price, add more input; if MVP < input price, use less; stop where MVP = input price.
Do not confuse the maximum TOTAL product (9 kg at 5 kg/ha) with the maximum PROFIT (3 kg/ha).

similar_questions.stem: Using textbook Table 4.3 (maize price 5 Nkf/kg, fertilizer 15 Nkf/kg): TP = 10, 14, 20, 28, 32, 35, 36, 35 kg/ha at 0–7 kg fertilizer. Find the MP at 3 kg, the MVP at 3 kg, and the profit-maximizing fertilizer level.
similar_questions.answer: MP at 3 kg = 28 − 20 = 8 kg; MVP = 8 × 5 = 40 Nkf; MVP column = 20, 30, 40, 20, 15, 5, −5 → MVP = 15 = fertilizer price at 5 kg/ha, so 5 kg/ha maximizes profit.
explanation_steps: MVP = MP × price of maize.
Profit-maximizing input level: MVP = price of input (15 Nkf) at 5 kg/ha.

questions.stem:
Write short notes about the following terms: (2 points)
A) Enclosure/closure   B) Nursery
questions.answer: A) Enclosure (closure): an area – usually a steep, degraded hillside – put under full or partial protection by restricting human activities such as livestock grazing and tree cutting for a number of years so that natural vegetation regenerates; it reduces erosion and runoff, increases infiltration and protects local flora and fauna. B) Nursery: a place where seedlings (of trees, fruits, vegetables, ornamentals) are raised and cared for under controlled conditions until they are ready for transplanting to the field; types are peasant, standard (commercial) and intermediate/temporary nurseries.
explanation_steps: Textbook 2.2.8: 'Enclosure or closure means an area that has been put under full or partial protection by restricting human-induced activities such as livestock grazing.' Usually on steep slopes, until natural vegetation re-grows.

Textbook 3.5.3: nurseries raise seedlings; peasant nursery (farmers raise their own seedlings), standard nursery (commercial production), intermediate/temporary nursery (holding previously raised seedlings near the planting site).
marking_points: Enclosure: area protected from grazing/cutting so natural vegetation regenerates (degraded, steep land) (1)
Nursery: place where seedlings are raised and cared for until transplanting (1)
tips: For 1 point each: definition + one purpose/example.

similar_questions.stem: Write short notes on afforestation and reforestation.
similar_questions.answer: Afforestation – establishing a forest (planting trees) on land that has not had forest for a long time or never had it. Reforestation – replanting trees on land where a forest was recently cut or destroyed.
explanation_steps: Both are discussed in Grade 12, 2.2.5 Afforestation and Reforestation.

questions.stem: Draw and explain the soil profile using a diagram. (4 points)
questions.answer: Diagram: a vertical section with layers from top to bottom – O, A, B, C horizons resting on R (bedrock). O-horizon: surface organic layer of leaf litter and roots, not saturated with water (common in forests and grasslands). A-horizon (topsoil): mineral layer at or near the surface mixed with humified organic matter; dark, most biological activity and roots; zone of leaching (eluviation). B-horizon (subsoil): zone of accumulation (illuviation) of clay, iron, aluminium and organic matter washed down from above, and/or weathering of the parent material. C-horizon: unconsolidated or weakly consolidated, weathered parent material that still shows rock structure and is little affected by soil-forming processes. R: unweathered bedrock. A soil profile is the vertical cross-section of the soil through all its horizons into the parent material.
explanation_steps: Definition (textbook): a soil profile is the vertical cross-sectional view of the soil through all its horizons extending into the parent material; horizons are layers roughly parallel to the surface.
The master horizons are O, A, B and C (textbook 2.2.2); bedrock (R) lies below.
Draw a labelled rectangle divided into horizontal bands: O (thin, dark litter) → A (dark topsoil) → B (lighter/reddish subsoil) → C (broken rock fragments) → R (solid rock).
Explain each horizon in one line using the textbook descriptions.
marking_points: Correctly ordered, labelled diagram showing O, A, B, C (R) horizons (1)
O/A horizons explained: organic litter; humus-rich topsoil (1)
B horizon explained: subsoil, accumulation/illuviation of clay, Fe, Al, organic matter (1)
C horizon (and R) explained: weathered parent material over bedrock (1)
tips: Marks usually: correct diagram with labels (1–2) + explanation of the horizons (2–3).
Order matters: O at the top, C/R at the bottom.

similar_questions.stem: Why do sandy parent materials develop a mature soil profile faster than clay soils?
similar_questions.answer: Water moves quickly through sandy material, and profile development depends on water moving through the soil; sands also contain few soluble materials. Clay soils drain slowly, so their profiles mature more slowly.
explanation_steps: Textbook 2.2.2: mature profile development depends on the capacity of water to move through the profile.
